issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma in a 34-year-old Navy Officer, 'Known People: Related people' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger without any accompanying memory or appraisal content about bereavement, loss of specific others, or interpersonal aspects of the disaster. The rest of the profile does not explain why related people would be a salient trigger.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. It suggests social/performance shame concerns, but the negative appraisals and memory items do not involve appearance, performance failure, humiliation, or social judgment. This maladaptive strategy appears to address a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

'Avoid Friends' similarly implies socially driven withdrawal, yet the selected appraisals are global despair and alienation rather than fear of specific interpersonal consequences, and the trigger set does not include friendship or social contact themes. It is not impossible, but in combination with 'Avoid Evaluation' it pulls toward a social-evaluative formulation not supported elsewhere.

For a natural-disaster trauma in a Navy officer, 'Similar cars' is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the profile. The other triggers are generic situational reminders (crowding, locations), but this item implies a specific vehicle-related cue that is not supported by the trauma type, memory content, or appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are extremely global and severe ('life not worth living', 'belong nowhere') relative to the rest of the selected items, which focus on trauma reminders, fragmented imagery, and avoidance. This creates a coherence problem because the profile lacks corresponding threat content or broader self-concept material to support such pervasive suicidal/existential beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is especially difficult to reconcile with the demographic/contextual profile of a married Navy officer after a natural disaster unless other items indicate moral injury, social alienation, or occupational rupture; none are present in the selected components.

vignette:
Lieutenant Commander Marcus Cole was thirty-four years old, a decorated Navy officer who had served on destroyers and guided-missile cruisers, a man who had always prided himself on his composure under pressure. That composure had been tested three years earlier when his ship, the USS Vanguard, was caught in a Category 4 typhoon in the Philippine Sea. He had been the officer of the deck during the worst of it, responsible for the safety of three hundred sailors as the ship rolled forty degrees and waves crashed over the bow. He remembered the screaming of the wind, the shuddering of the hull, the moment a rogue wave smashed a porthole and seawater flooded the berthing compartment, and the hours of scrambling to secure hatches and rescue a young seaman who had been swept against a bulkhead. What stayed with him most, though, was not the chaos but the stillness afterward—the way his hands had trembled uncontrollably for an hour, the way he had stared at his own reflection in a dark window and not recognized the man looking back.

In the months that followed, Marcus found himself avoiding things he could not explain. He stopped going to the base gym because it was too crowded; he started taking the long way to his office to avoid the narrow corridor near the mess hall. The conviction that he deserved to suffer meant that the memory of the flooded berthing compartment surfaced almost daily now, each time more vivid than the last — as if his guilt had sharpened it into a weapon he kept turning over in his hands. When his wife suggested a weekend trip to the city, he made excuses about work. He began drinking alone in the evenings, a habit he had never had before, and the smell of alcohol on his own breath would sometimes bring the typhoon rushing back—the metallic tang of seawater, the acrid odor of diesel fuel, the sour sweat of fear. On those nights, he would sit in the dark of his garage, his body rigid, his hands clenched into fists, feeling as though he were still braced against that endless roll. The memory felt so extreme, so impossible, that he sometimes had to remind himself it had really happened. He would replay the images—the flooded berthing, the seaman’s terrified face, the shuddering metal—and each time, he would think, I should have done more. I deserve this. That same belief — that he deserved what had happened — began to expand the range of things that could trigger him: now even the sound of running water from a faucet or the sight of a puddle on the pavement would snap his attention back to the ship, because his guilt had taught him to see the typhoon everywhere.

Marcus had come to believe that he no longer belonged anywhere. At work, his fellow officers seemed distant, their conversations about football and fishing trivial and hollow. He felt isolated, set apart, as if a pane of glass separated him from everyone else. He used to be a happy person, he was certain of that—but now he was always miserable, and he could not remember when that had changed. When a memory surfaced, triggered by a sudden gust of wind or a dark hallway, he would feel his body lock into that same position: feet planted, knees bent, hands gripping an invisible railing. And then the isolation would deepen, because how could anyone understand what it had been like? He told himself he deserved to suffer, and so he stopped answering calls from his old shipmates, stopped accepting invitations to barbecues, stopped walking past the base chapel where he used to sit and think. Each avoidance made the memories feel more unreal, more like a story that had happened to someone else, and the more unreal they felt, the more he felt he had to punish himself for not being able to let it go. Not talking about it, never letting himself describe it aloud, meant the memory had never been put into words — it remained in him, undisturbed and intact, exactly where he had left it, waiting to be replayed in full.

The loop tightened over months. A crowded commissary would send him home early, and at home the darkness of the bedroom would bring back the typhoon, and the typhoon would bring the guilt, and the guilt would drive him to the garage where he would sit in the dark and think, This is where I belong. He began to notice that any physical location that reminded him of the ship—a narrow hallway, a room with no windows, a floor that vibrated—would trigger the same bodily reenactment, and then the same spiral of self-blame. He avoided those places, but the avoidance itself became a trigger: every time he took a different route, every time he said no to an invitation, the memory returned, sharper and more punishing. Each place he avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round he drove to avoid the bridge was its own daily acknowledgement of the typhoon, and the act of rerouting brought the event back into his mind as surely as any direct encounter would have. He was certain that if he stopped avoiding, something terrible would happen—that he would fall apart, that his wife would see what he had become, that the Navy would discharge him.

What finally brought Marcus to the clinic was a minor thing. His wife had asked him to pick up takeout from a restaurant near the waterfront, and he had driven forty minutes out of his way to avoid the bridge. When he came home, she was crying. She said she did not know who he was anymore. He sat on the edge of the bed, his hands trembling, and he thought about the seaman he had pulled from the flood—how the man had thanked him, how Marcus had said It’s my job—and he realized he could not remember the last time he had felt that simple, that clear. He was afraid of what would happen if he stopped punishing himself. He was more afraid of what would happen if he did not.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to memory; the vignette describes memory triggering guilt, but not guilt strengthening the memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to triggers; the vignette does not show guilt or self-blame causing new triggers to appear.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies lead to memory; avoidance is described as triggered by memory, but not as causing or strengthening the memory.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies lead to triggers; avoidance is described as a response to triggers, not as generating new triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
